item.title: Foxconn India unit faces $15 mn insolvency suit over unpaid vendor dues
item.description: BCD Emprasa LLP, which leased dormitory housing in southern India for the Foxconn unit's employees at the Bengaluru facility, has alleged that it didn't receive payment for rent and utilities ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Alisha Sachdev About half a dozen vendors in India are experiencing payment delays by Foxconn Technology Group’s local unit, said people familiar with the matter, with one even filing an insolvency lawsuit to recover $15 million in unpaid dues. BCD Emprasa LLP, which leased dormitory housing in southern India for the Foxconn unit’s employees at the Bengaluru facility, has alleged that it didn’t receive payment for rent and utilities in an Aug. 12 petition to the National Company Law Tribunal’s Chennai bench. The company is seeking about ₹143 crore ($15.3 million) for past dues along with interest, service charges and damages as of July 8 from Foxconn Hon Hai Technology India Mega Development Pvt., according to the filing, which was seen by Bloomberg News. Vendors in India often initiate insolvency proceedings to recover overdue payments, though these filings rarely push a company into bankruptcy.  While the dispute isn’t expected to derail Foxconn’s growth plans in India, it adds to the challenges facing the iPhone assembler as it competes with Tata Electronics Pvt. for a bigger role in Apple Inc.’s supply chain. Bloomberg News reported last year that Foxconn recalled hundreds of Chinese workers from India — though the reason wasn’t clear at the time — in a move that saw the company bring in staff from Taiwan and Vietnam to minimize the impact on production. Foxconn didn’t reply to emailed queries seeking comments on BCD’s lawsuit in India.  “These defaults have caused grave financial prejudice and substantial commercial harm to the company” BCD said in an emailed response, adding that the matter was sub judice before NCLT. At least four vendors other than BCD have been waiting for several months to over a year for Foxconn to clear their dues, said people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing private information. Several were hired for construction-related work on the Bengaluru facility and were working with Foxconn for the first time. Under an April 2024 agreement with BCD, Foxconn leased 700 residential units for female employees, with rent payable regardless of occupancy and a lock-in through July 2026, according to the NCLT filing. Foxconn defaulted on an invoice due in May 2025, it said. The electronics giant also did not agree to appointing an arbitrator. Departures of some non-Indian staff have slowed payments to local contractors, the people said.

item.title: Oil prices fall as supply glut concerns offset West Asia disruption fears
item.description: Brent crude futures fell 43 cents, or 0.5%, to $90.97 a barrel by 0137 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures slipped 47 cents, or 0.6%, to $81.58 a barrel ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / Commodities / Oil prices fall as supply glut concerns offset West Asia disruption fears

Oil prices fall as supply glut concerns offset West Asia disruption fears Brent crude futures fell 43 cents, or 0.5%, to $90.97 a barrel by 0137 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures slipped 47 cents, or 0.6%, to $81.58 a barrel

Both benchmarks gained more than 2% on Tuesday | Image: Bloomberg

Reuters TOKYO 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 25 2026 | 8:08 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Crude oil prices fell on Wednesday, paring some of the previous day's gains, as concerns over supply disruptions in the West Asia were offset by rising supply and the prospect of a market surplus. Brent crude futures fell 43 cents, or 0.5%, to $90.97 a barrel by 0137 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures slipped 47 cents, or 0.6%, to $81.58 a barrel. Both benchmarks gained more than 2% on Tuesday. "Since the release of an IEA report this month, perceptions of a global supply glut have kept prices in check," said Tsuyoshi Ueno, senior economist at NLI Research Institute. "However, attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz and exchanges of attacks between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis have raised uncertainty over the sustainability of this trend," he said.

Also Read

Attention is also focused on how next year's production quotas will be determined at the Opec+ meeting, Ueno added. Opec+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The International Energy Agency said on November 13 that the world oil market would return to a surplus in the fourth quarter as West Asia exports recover faster than global oil demand. Libya's Sharara oil pipeline has reopened after an "unlawful group" closed a valve on the pipeline, with oil beginning to flow into storage tanks at the Akakus facility in Zawiya, the chairperson of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Monday.

Iraq is pressing Opec+ to lift its estimate of the country's crude oil production capacity, four people familiar with the matter said, heightening tensions over a review that will help determine how much members can pump next year. China and India are on track for record Russian oil imports this year, plugging a supply gap caused by the Iran war, according to tanker data and industry sources. Meanwhile, a container ship was targeted while sailing an "unauthorised" route near the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said, according to state media. On Monday, three vessels were struck by unidentified projectiles as they sailed east through the strait, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Tuesday.

US crude stocks rose by 126,000 barrels in the week ended November 20, market sources said on Tuesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute.  Eight analysts polled by Reuters estimated that crude inventories rose by about 1.5 million barrels on average.

item.title: Iran slams US over unpaid OPCW dues, warns of threat to global security
item.description: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has accused Washington of undermining the OPCW through unpaid dues, warning that the funding crisis could disrupt its operations ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Iran slams US over unpaid OPCW dues, warns of threat to global security

Iran slams US over unpaid OPCW dues, warns of threat to global security Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has accused Washington of undermining the OPCW through unpaid dues, warning that the funding crisis could disrupt its operations

Abbas Araghchi, Iran's foreign minister | Image Credit: Bloomberg

ANI 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 25 2026 | 7:59 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi on Tuesday criticised the United States for allegedly undermining the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), warning that unpaid US dues are threatening the global watchdog's operations. In a post on X, Araghchi accused Washington of hypocrisy regarding chemical arms. "The US is so concerned about chemical arms that it's crippling the world's chemical weapons watchdog," he wrote. He noted that the OPCW may be forced to suspend work and scale back vital programs, adding that by "obstructing its mandate, the US is deliberately putting global peace and security at risk". Araghchi described the situation as "shameful".

Araghchi's remarks accompanied a screenshot of a Reuters report titled, "US arrears leave chemical weapons watchdog facing budget crisis". Also Read

Vance, Rubio meet Qatar PM as uncertainty grows over Trump's Iran plans

India's influence grows despite economic dip as US-China power gap shrinks

Trump suggests Iran strikes could resume next year if peace talks fail

The post also quoted an earlier statement made by Araghchi on November 17, in which he dismissed recent media reports alleging that Iran was plotting to use chemical weapons in Washington, DC, while constructing missile bases beneath dams. Characterising those reports as "pro-Israel media" narratives and "Iraq War-style propaganda," Araghchi flatly rejected the claims as "RUBBISH". Earlier, US President Donald Trump said he is inclined to launch military strikes on Iran after the New Year if a deal is not reached, Fox News reported.

Calling the Iranian side "professional tap dancers", Trump criticised its approach to negotiations, saying Tehran kept talking without making tangible progress. "They talk all the time. All they do is talk, but it's all BS," Trump was quoted as saying by Fox News. "I hope Iranian tankers try to test the blockade. They will all be at the bottom of the sea, like Iran's navy," he said. The latest remarks come amid continuing tensions between Washington and Tehran, with Trump repeatedly expressing dissatisfaction over the terms Iran has been willing to offer in negotiations.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Houthis close in on Aden as Yemeni forces dig in behind fortified line

Houthis close in on Aden as Yemeni forces dig in behind fortified line The Houthis' advance toward Aden has come after forces allied with the government withdrew from areas on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, allowing the Houthis to consolidate their grip on territory

Houthi supporters gather in Yemen’s capital Sana’a as fighting intensifies across several fronts. | Photo: Reuters

AP Dubai 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 25 2026 | 7:52 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Iran-backed Houthi rebels have advanced to within about 60 kilometres of the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government in the southern city of Aden, but the forces fighting them have set up a fortified line to defend the city, a military official said Tuesday. Iran reiterated Tuesday that it would not hold talks with the United States to end their conflict unless several conditions are met. It also said three oil tankers had struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire despite US aerial protection. Meanwhile, at least nine Palestinians were killed in several Israeli strikes in Gaza, local officials said.

Houthi rebels advance toward Aden The Houthis' advance toward Aden has come after forces allied with the government withdrew from areas on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, allowing the Houthis to consolidate their grip on territory around the crucial waterway. Col. Majed al-Nuzaily, spokesman for the Yemeni army, said the forces that withdrew from the western coast are now stationed north and west of Aden "on a defence line built to stop the Houthi advance," as the rebels come within 60 kilometers of the city. Also Read

CONFLICT ZONE: Yemen premium

"Aden is a red line. It was a red line in 2015, when the Houthis came to the city and its people drove them out," he said during a virtual briefing.

Speaking in the same briefing, Yemeni foreign ministry official Marwan al-Noman called for the United States and other Western countries to support the Yemeni coast guard in its efforts to intercept smuggled weapons to the Houthis, as well as provide training to Yemeni forces fighting the rebels on the ground. "The Houthis are a terrorist organisation. They threaten Yemenis first, and then every nation whose ships cross the Red Sea," he said. Officials say a child is among those killed in Yemen Yemen's Interior Ministry said Tuesday that shelling of areas in Taiz province in southwestern Yemen killed three civilians, including a child, and wounded two other children, citing local police.

The ministry, which is aligned with Yemen's internationally recognised government, blamed the Houthis for the attack. The Houthis and the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen continue to trade accusations that civilians in their respective territories have been targeted in recent hostilities.
